annotations.keyFindings: A carbon monoxide alarm sounded when tested in 37 percent of 661 rural households although 61 percent reported owning one; working smoke alarms were found in 78 percent.
annotations.limitations: One region with a different housing stock; nonresponse was higher in rented homes; hallway and kitchen only.

annotations.keyFindings: Nationally, a carbon monoxide alarm was recorded in 44 percent of dwellings with a fuel-burning appliance, without a sound test; coverage was lowest in older privately rented dwellings.
annotations.limitations: Dominated by urban housing; presence recorded without testing.

annotations.keyFindings: Working carbon monoxide alarms were present in 28 percent of privately rented and 44 percent of owner-occupied rural homes, a prevalence ratio of 0.64, with the widest gap in homes heated with bottled gas.
annotations.limitations: Two districts; tenure reported by the respondent; 49 percent response.

annotations.keyFindings: Door-to-door recruitment reached 61 percent of sampled renters against 29 percent by telephone, and the telephone sample overstated working alarm prevalence by 9 points after weighting.
annotations.limitations: Urban and suburban sample; costs not reported.

annotations.keyFindings: Renters made up 12 percent of requested home safety visits against 27 percent of households.
annotations.limitations: Descriptive service data from one fire service.

annotations.keyFindings: In 33 of 41 rural carbon monoxide deaths the home had no working alarm; 24 involved solid fuel or bottled gas appliances.

claims.text: In two rural districts, working carbon monoxide alarms were present in 28 percent of privately rented homes and 44 percent of owner-occupied homes.
claims.passage: Working carbon monoxide alarms were present in 28 percent of privately rented homes and 44 percent of owner-occupied homes (prevalence ratio 0.64).
claims.interpretation: Planning value for the tenure comparison; two districts only.

claims.text: In a door-to-door rural survey, a carbon monoxide alarm sounded when tested in 37 percent of households although 61 percent said they owned one.
claims.passage: A carbon monoxide alarm sounded when tested in 37 percent of households, although 61 percent said they owned one.
claims.interpretation: Self-report overstates working alarms; verification is needed.

claims.text: Door-to-door recruitment reached 61 percent of sampled renters compared with 29 percent by telephone.
claims.passage: Door-to-door recruitment reached 61 percent of sampled renters compared with 29 percent by telephone.
claims.interpretation: Door-to-door fieldwork is needed to reach renters.

synthesis: Six retrieved records, appraised at abstract level. Tested working carbon monoxide alarms are much less common than reported ownership (37 against 61 percent in one rural survey), rented homes had fewer working alarms than owner-occupied homes in two rural districts (28 against 44 percent), and door-to-door recruitment reached renters far better than telephone. A national survey recorded carbon monoxide alarms in 44 percent of dwellings with a fuel-burning appliance without testing them. The 40 percent figure quoted locally matches no retrieved record.
gradeRationale: Descriptive surveys with moderate response from a few areas, a national survey without sound tests, and grey service data; consistent in direction but imprecise for this county.
summary: Six retrieved records appraised; three source-derived claims recorded with passages.
